body: A spectrometer separates radiation by wavelength and measures how much arrives in different bands. A hot dense object can give a broad spectrum. A dilute excited gas can emit strongly at particular wavelengths, appearing as bright lines in a graph or image.

When broad-spectrum light passes through a cooler gas, some wavelengths can be absorbed more strongly, appearing as dark lines. Comparing observed patterns with laboratory spectra helps identify atoms or molecules along the path. A spectrum of a star therefore gives evidence beyond the color seen by an eye.
credit: Centauri Archive editorial draft, written with AI assistance
limitations: Multiple substances and physical conditions can contribute to the same observation. Motion can shift wavelengths and finite instrument resolution can blend lines. A single line may not identify its source.
purpose: Show what a measurement across wavelengths can reveal about a source.
